entry.title: MosaicML Composer: A Source Tour of Event-Driven Speedup Training

link.title: MosaicML Composer: A Source Tour of Event-Driven Speedup Training

entry.content:
MosaicML composer is an open-source PyTorch training library built around one idea: if you can observe training as a sequence of well-defined moments, you can intervene at those moments to make models train faster without changing the math of your model. The library packages dozens of researched “speedup methods” — ColOut, BlurPool, SelectiveBackprop, EMA, SeqLengthWarmup, and more — as first-class objects that plug into a shared life cycle. Rather than scattering hacks through your training script, composer lets you list methods by name and trust the framework to fire them at exactly the right instant.

Why does the source deserve a tour? Because composer is one of the cleanest public examples of event-driven training architecture in the PyTorch ecosystem. The Trainer owns the loop; the Engine walks a strict Event enum and asks every Algorithm and Callback whether it wants to act; a State object carries the model, optimizers, schedulers, and timers so every participant reads and writes the same truth. Once you see how that event chain is wired, you will recognize the same pattern in larger systems, and you will understand exactly where your own hooks would go. It also pairs naturally with the tooling we have covered before: PyTorch supplies the tensors and autograd underneath, DeepSpeed and Accelerate cover other sharding and launch styles, and Flash-Attention is one kernel-level optimization that composer-style methods complement rather than replace.

In this post we read the actual code from the main branch: the trainer loop in composer/trainer/trainer.py, the dispatch machinery in composer/core/engine.py, real algorithm implementations under composer/algorithms/, the callback and logger packages, and the distributed sync helpers. Two diagrams map the territory — one coarse, one detailed.

The composer system at a glance: a Trainer loop feeds an event engine that dispatches to algorithms, callbacks, and distributed sync helpers.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The Trainer, L526 class is the front door. Its constructor at init, L1003 assembles the State, the logger, the engine, and every callback you registered, so by the time training starts the whole object graph exists.
  • fit, L1933 is the public entry point. It normalizes durations, validates your configuration, and then launches the private loop below it.
  • The real rhythm lives in _train_loop, L2383, which emits FIT_START, EPOCH_START, BATCH_START, ITERATION_END, and their siblings — one run_event call per life-cycle moment.
  • Those calls land in the Engine, L175, whose run_event, L227 method iterates over registered algorithms and callbacks for the given Event, L10 value.
  • The State, L257 object is the shared blackboard: model, optimizers, learning-rate schedulers, dataloaders, and timestamps all live here, which is why a single Algorithm.apply can reshape training mid-flight.
  • On the speedup side, the Algorithm, L20 base class defines the match/apply contract, and concrete methods such as ColOut, L162 and BlurPool, L81 implement it.
  • Observability comes from SpeedMonitor, L171, which reads timings from state and pushes them through the Logger, L26 facade into any destination you configured.
  • Finally, on multiple workers, ddp_sync_context, L74 decides when gradient all-reduce happens, trading communication frequency for throughput.

From Install to Your First Model

Composer installs like any PyTorch companion package. pip install mosaicml pulls the library plus its core dependencies; pip install 'mosaicml[tensorboard]' or pip install 'mosaicml[wandb]' adds logger extras. There is no separate compile step and no plugin registration ritual — speedup methods and callbacks are ordinary Python classes exported from the composer namespace.

A minimal fit looks like this:

from composer import Trainer, algorithms, callbacks

trainer = Trainer(
    model=model,
    train_dataloader=train_dl,
    eval_dataloader=eval_dl,
    max_duration="2ep",
    algorithms=[
        algorithms.ColOut(),
        algorithms.BlurPool(),
        algorithms.SeqLengthWarmup(duration=0.3),
    ],
    callbacks=[callbacks.SpeedMonitor(window_size=100)],
    loggers=[],
)
trainer.fit()

The interesting part is that nothing above mentions when each method runs. ColOut declares internally that it acts on Event.FIT_START (it shrinks both image rows/columns and the batch size proportionally), BlurPool asks to be re-applied after model construction, and SeqLengthWarmup edits sequence length during the early fraction of training. The Trainer collects their preferences at init, and the engine honors them for the rest of the run. That declaration-over-orchestration style is the library’s signature: your script lists what, the framework owns when. If you have used Hugging Face tooling, the mental model transfers directly — see our Transformers tour for that side of the fence.

The Event Chain: How Algorithms Meet Training

The detail diagram zooms into the dispatch machinery, which is the heart of the codebase.

Detailed view: run_event walks the Event enum, filters algorithms through match(), applies them to State, and notifies callbacks that fan results into loggers.

Every call to Engine.run_event performs two passes in a fixed order. First _run_algorithms (line 381 of engine.py) consults each algorithm’s match(event, state) hook — declared at match, L71 — and invokes apply (defined at apply, L103) on everything that matches. Second, _run_callbacks (line 464) calls the method named after the event on each Callback — the base class at Callback, L19 provides an empty default for all of them, so subclasses override only what they need. Algorithms may mutate the model graph; callbacks are strictly observers and reporters.

The loop code in _train_loop shows the chain in context. Around BATCH_START the trainer wraps the batch in a ddp_sync_context chosen by the DDPSyncStrategy enum at DDPSyncStrategy, L44 — single_auto syncs once per batch, while multi-microbatch strategies defer the all-reduce so gradient accumulation stays cheap. Then BEFORE_FORWARD, AFTER_FORWARD, BEFORE_LOSS, AFTER_LOSS, BEFORE_BACKWARD, and AFTER_BACKWARD bracket the actual tensor work, with AFTER_TRAIN_BATCH and BATCH_END closing each step. Eval reuses the identical machinery with an EVAL_* family of events driven from _eval_loop (line 3314 of trainer.py). Checkpointing is just another event pair — BATCH_CHECKPOINT and EPOCH_CHECKPOINT — which is why resuming an interrupted run needs no special-case code.

Time itself is first-class here. The Time class at Time, L83 models durations in epochs, batches, samples, or tokens, and Timestamp, L461 snapshots how much of each unit has elapsed. Because durations can be declared as strings like '2ep' or '5000ba' and converted internally, the trainer decides when to stop without the loop knowing which unit you meant. This is also what makes fractional durations such as the 0.3 in SeqLengthWarmup work: the engine compares fractional progress on a shared clock rather than guessing from raw iteration counts, so a warmup stays correct whether the run lasts two epochs or twenty.

Speedup Methods Worth Knowing

The composer/algorithms/ directory is the library’s research catalog, each subpackage with its own README, metadata, and tests. A few illustrate the range:

  • ColOut, L162 drops a small percentage of rows and columns from every image and the same percentage of examples from each batch, shrinking total FLOPs by roughly the square of the image reduction. Accuracy stays close because information loss is spread thinly.
  • BlurPool, L81 rewrites strided convolutions to blur before subsampling, preserving shift invariance — a classic method from the “Making Convolutional Networks Shift-Invariant Again” paper, productized here as an apply-once model edit.
  • SelectiveBackprop, L171 ranks the examples in a batch by current loss, runs the backward pass only on the hardest fraction, and skips the easy ones — cutting gradient compute when the dataset has many trivially learnable samples.
  • EMA, L96 maintains an exponential moving average of weights on AFTER_BACKWARD, usually improving final eval metrics for a tiny memory cost.
  • GatedLinearUnits, L169 and SeqLengthWarmup, L152 target transformer training: the former swaps FFN blocks for gated variants, the latter starts training on short sequences and ramps up, front-loading the cheapest tokens first.
  • LayerFreezing, L92 freezes low-value layers as training progresses, shrinking backward cost late in the run.

When the trainer shortens a schedule — for example because ColOut effectively reduced total work — it calls scale_pytorch_scheduler, L16 so native PyTorch LR schedulers see a rescaled timeline instead of drifting out of sync. Small detail, but it shows how much of the library’s correctness lives in bookkeeping.

Callbacks, Logging, and Distributed Sync

Callbacks are the observability half of the event chain. SpeedMonitor, L171 accumulates wall-clock and throughput statistics in batch_end and reports them over a rolling window; LRMonitor, L11 logs the learning rate of every optimizer each batch; and CheckpointSaver, L45 persists full training state on a cadence you configure, delegating to the trainer’s save_checkpoint method (line 3661 of trainer.py). All of them subclass the same passive Callback base and stay out of the training path unless fired.

Logging is a two-layer design. The Logger facade fans every call out to LoggerDestination objects; composer ships destinations for TensorBoard, Weights & Biases, Comet, MLflow, Neptune, Slack, console output, and a handy InMemoryLogger, L27 that stores timeseries in a dict — ideal for tests, notebooks, and ConsoleLogger, L27-style quick inspection. Because callbacks receive the same Logger, a single speed_monitor line of logging surfaces in every destination at once. On the distributed side, helpers in composer/utils/dist.py (such as get_world_size, line 212) abstract rank and world-size queries so the trainer code reads the same on one GPU or sixty-four.

The profiler follows the same pattern. The Profiler class at Profiler, L30 is itself a callback: it schedules profiling windows, wraps torch.profiler, and writes Chrome-style traces through handlers living in the same package. Because it hooks the shared event chain, you enable it with one constructor argument and read results without ever touching the loop. Other ready-made observers in composer/callbacks/ include a memory monitor and a system metrics collector, plus an early stopper and a threshold stopper — each a small file that reacts to events and nothing more. If you ever need your own observability, copying one of these compact callbacks is the gentlest possible introduction to extending the framework.

Honest Limits

Composer’s strengths are real, but so are the caveats. First, the speedup numbers are workload-dependent: methods tuned for vision CNNs (BlurPool) do nothing for a transformer, and text-only methods (SeqLengthWarmup) are irrelevant to image classifiers — you must pick a coherent subset, not enable everything. Second, some algorithms change semantics (SelectiveBackprop skips gradients for easy examples), so loss curves will differ from a vanilla run and ablations remain your responsibility. Third, the library has evolved quickly — DeepSpeed-specific integration once lived under composer/trainer/ but the distributed strategies now live in composer/distributed/, so older blog snippets and tutorials drift out of date; always check the branch you are reading. Fourth, composer is heavier than a bare PyTorch loop: the event machinery is worth it at scale, but for a five-minute experiment on one GPU, plain PyTorch with a hand-written loop can be simpler. Finally, the Trainer is opinionated about orchestration — if your project needs a fully custom optimization regime, you may spend more time fighting State assumptions than writing your own loop. None of this diminishes the architecture: as a study of how to make training extensible without chaos, composer remains one of the best codebases in the ecosystem.
entry.summary: Walk through the MosaicML composer source: the Trainer loop, the Engine event chain, speedup algorithms, callbacks, logging, and distributed sync.

entry.title: Hugging Face Datasets Source Tour: From load_dataset to Arrow Shards

link.title: Hugging Face Datasets Source Tour: From load_dataset to Arrow Shards

entry.content:
If you have trained a model on a public corpus in the last five years, the odds are very high that the data reached you through huggingface/datasets. The library is the de facto data layer of the open-source model ecosystem: one call to load_dataset pulls a named dataset from the Hub, converts it to Arrow, caches it under your home directory, and returns an object you can index, filter, shuffle, and hand straight to a training loop. The model-loading side of that ecosystem is covered in our Transformers tour, and the tokenization layer in the Tokenizers walkthrough — datasets is the quieter component that feeds both of them every single day.

The source deserves a careful read because the library makes a series of pragmatic engineering decisions that show up directly in your own projects: content-addressed caches made of hash-named folders, memory-mapped Arrow files that allow zero-copy reads from many worker processes, and fingerprinted transformations so the output of an expensive map survives across sessions. Once you understand how those pieces connect, mysterious disk usage and re-downloads stop being mysterious — they become predictable consequences of a design you can point at line by line. That is exactly what this post is for.

Our tour follows a stage-wise flow through the repository at its current main branch: public entry points, then the discovery stage that turns glob patterns into concrete files, then the builder stage that downloads sources and generates examples, then the Arrow layer that writes and reads shards, and finally the in-memory objects you actually hold in a notebook. Read together, they describe one continuous arrow data flow from a URL on the Hub to a typed table inside your Python process. Every symbol link below was checked against the checked-out HEAD before publishing, so the line anchors are real.

What the Library Actually Ships

The first surprise in src/datasets is how flat the core is. There is no tall stack of abstractions: arrow_dataset.py is a single very large module holding the eager Dataset class and its transformations, load.py contains the user-facing resolution logic, and builder.py defines the DatasetBuilder base class that every format-specific builder extends. Network behavior is quarantined in the download/ subpackage, which separates DownloadManager, StreamingDownloadManager, and DownloadConfig from everything else — a clean seam that keeps the rest of the code testable without touching the network.

Around that core sit three supporting rings. The packaged_modules/ tree contains ready-made builders for parquet, CSV, JSON, imagefolder, audiofolder, and dozens of other formats; the Parquet builder at Parquet, L93 is the one most Hub repositories hit today. Metadata lives in info.py and splits.py, while the typed column schema — including audio, image, and video columns — is defined in Features, L1923. Runtime constants such as the cache root live in config.py, starting with HF_DATASETS_CACHE, L161.

The Overview, Stage by Stage

The overview diagram traces the arrow data flow from load_dataset through builder caching to the Dataset objects returned to the caller.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • The public entry point is load_dataset, L1446, which normalizes arguments and decides between an eager DatasetDict, a single Dataset, or a lazy streaming variant.
  • It delegates resolution to load_dataset_builder, L1187, which imports the right builder module and instantiates it with your configuration.
  • When you pass local files, the discovery stage calls into DataFilesDict, L650, which resolves glob patterns and Hub URLs into a concrete, sorted list of source files.
  • The build stage is anchored by DatasetBuilder, L214, whose download_and_prepare, L702 method orchestrates the entire caching run and skips work when the cache is already valid.
  • Fetching itself is the job of DownloadManager, L71, which hands the author-defined split hook a small API for requesting URLs and archives.
  • Generated examples are serialized by ArrowWriter, L514, which infers a schema from the first examples and appends rows into Arrow shard files on disk.
  • On the way back out, ArrowReader, L285 rebuilds tables from those shards; nothing re-runs the generators when the cache is warm.
  • Finally Dataset, L709 wraps the materialized table, and DatasetDict, L53 maps split names such as train and test onto those objects.

The important property of this flow is that it is resumable at every stage. The download cache, the generated Arrow cache, and the fingerprint cache are three separate layers, each with its own invalidation rule, so a failed run usually costs you only the unfinished stage rather than the whole preparation.

From Install to Your First Model

Installation is deliberately boring: pip install datasets brings in PyArrow, huggingface-hub, and a handful of small dependencies. Your first real interaction looks like this:

from datasets import load_dataset

ds = load_dataset("ag_news")
print(ds["train"][0]["text"][:120])

One line hides the whole stage-wise flow from the overview. The library resolves ag_news on the Hub, downloads and unpacks its parquet shards through the download layer, writes an Arrow copy into your cache, and returns a DatasetDict of eager splits. Everything after that point reads from local disk: indexing a row is a memory-mapped lookup, not a network call, which is why you can share one cache across many experiments without ever re-downloading.

Transformations are where the design earns its keep. The map method at map, L3205 applies a function across rows and caches the result under a fingerprint derived from the function’s bytecode and closure; its sibling filter, L4134 is a predicate built on the same machinery, and shuffle, L4827 creates deterministic permutations that survive restarts. A typical preprocessing chain looks like this:

from transformers import AutoTokenizer
tok = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("distilbert-base-uncased")

ds = ds.map(lambda x: tok(x["text"]), batched=True)
ds = ds.with_format("torch")

Calling with_format, L2997 changes how rows are materialized — torch tensors, NumPy arrays, pandas frames, or JAX arrays — without copying the underlying Arrow table. That final tensor view is what you feed to a training loop built on PyTorch; the Arrow columns stay on disk and each batch is assembled lazily. If your per-row work is the expensive part, the fingerprint cache means the second run of the same map is nearly free, even in a fresh process.

Two more everyday methods round out the eager surface. train_test_split, L4967 carves deterministic holdout sets out of a single table, and select, L4359 builds a view over an explicit index list — both return new Dataset objects that share the parent’s Arrow memory until a transformation forces materialization. When your data starts as plain Python, from_dict, L983 converts a dictionary of lists into a full Dataset, inferring Features along the way. And once a cleaned version of a corpus is worth sharing, push_to_hub, L6070 uploads the Arrow shards and a generated README card back to the Hub, closing the loop between consumers and producers of data.

The Detail Diagram: One Call, Six Modules

The detail diagram expands the stage-wise flow into individual methods and shows how the download, build, Arrow, and in-memory layers interlock.

The detail view rewards a slow walk. Inside download_and_prepare, the builder first asks the author-defined hook _split_generators, L1197 for a plan; each returned SplitGenerator, L624 binds a split name to a shard key, and their byte counts end up registered in SplitDict, L530 inside the DatasetInfo record at DatasetInfo, L92. The download requests made inside that hook flow through cached_path, L129, which understands local paths, HTTP URLs, and Hub references, all tunable per call via DownloadConfig, L10.

The right half of the diagram shows the exit paths. The cached shards become objects through as_dataset, L991, which routes read_files, L254 results into Dataset instances; a completed folder can be re-opened later with load_from_disk after save_to_disk exports it, using the pair save_to_disk, L1781 and load_from_disk, L1704. The lazy alternative bypasses the Arrow cache entirely: in streaming mode, load_dataset returns IterableDataset, L2690, whose shard iteration is backed by the lazy StreamingDownloadManager, L47 and installed by extend_module_for_streaming, L42. Both modes share the same Features schema, so a dataset that streams can later be materialized with the same columns and types.

The writer side of the diagram deserves its own note. write_table, L804 appends each incoming batch to the current shard and rolls over at a configurable size, while finalize, L829 closes the file, writes the footer, and reports the byte and row totals that metadata later records. On the ingest side, download_and_extract, L310 chains fetching and unpacking for archives, and the split of responsibilities is strict: the builder decides what to generate, the manager decides where bytes come from, and the writer decides how they land on disk.

Honest Limits

The caching design has sharp edges worth naming. The Arrow cache is append-oriented: changing a builder configuration creates a new config id and therefore a new cache directory, and nothing garbage-collects the old one for you. Long experiment sessions can quietly accumulate dozens of gigabytes across ~/.cache/huggingface, so you should prune deliberately rather than discover the growth at the worst time. Fingerprint invalidation for map is conservative — it hashes the function’s bytecode, not its semantics — so editing a comment can invalidate a cache while editing a global constant may not, and there is no way to express fine-grained dependencies.

The eager Dataset also assumes its table fits comfortably on disk, and mostly in memory when you transform aggressively. map with num_proc multiplies memory pressure by worker count, and shuffling very wide tables can force the sort-based fallback that materializes indices. Streaming mode removes the disk cost but gives up random access, shuffling becomes a buffered approximation, and you cannot know the dataset length without an extra Hub query. Finally, datasets is a table cache with opinions, not a query engine: there is no SQL layer, no joins, and no server; complex relational work belongs in your own tooling, with datasets as the typed import and export layer. None of these are bugs — they are the documented cost of a design that puts resume-ability and speed ahead of everything else.

What you take away from the source is a set of transferable patterns: hash-addressed caches you can copy into any batch job, a builder contract that separates format authors from caching machinery, and an Arrow-first storage discipline that scales from a laptop to a training cluster. When you next reach for load_dataset, you will know precisely which lines run, in which order, and why your disk looks the way it does.
entry.summary: A source-level tour of huggingface/datasets: how load_dataset resolves a builder, caches Arrow shards on disk, and returns typed Dataset objects, with two architecture diagrams.

entry.title: Detectron2: A Source Tour of Meta’s Detection Platform

link.title: Detectron2: A Source Tour of Meta’s Detection Platform

entry.content:
Detectron2 is Meta AI Research’s next-generation library for object detection and segmentation, and it is the direct successor of the original Detectron and of maskrcnn-benchmark. Written in PyTorch, it has carried a whole generation of computer vision research: Faster and Mask R-CNN, panoptic segmentation, DensePose, Cascade R-CNN, PointRend, ViTDet, and a long tail of projects built on top of it. Unlike many model dumps that stop at weights and a training script, Detectron2 ships a genuinely readable reference implementation of the entire two-stage detection stack, which is why it remains one of the best codebases to study if you want to understand how modern detectors really work.

What makes the source so approachable is how small the load-bearing core is. One meta-architecture class, GeneralizedRCNN, L25, owns the end-to-end flow: it holds a backbone, a proposal generator, and ROI heads, and it simply wires them together. Everything else is a registry-driven factory: you pick a backbone by name, a proposal generator by name, ROI heads by name, and a yacs CfgNode tree supplies every constant, threshold, and channel count. That registry pattern is also why so many papers ship a Detectron2 config: the architecture description is data, not code. This tour reads that machinery as it exists on the main branch today, file by file, function by function.

Two diagrams accompany this post. The overview shows the ten-ish components you actually need to hold in your head; the detail graph zooms into the individual functions and their call relationships, from config ingestion down to anchor tiling and box decoding. Both link to real files in the repository.

Overview of Detectron2: the GeneralizedRCNN meta-architecture assembles a ResNet (optionally wrapped by FPN) backbone, an RPN proposal stage built on DefaultAnchorGenerator, and StandardROIHeads; DefaultPredictor and DefaultTrainer drive it, while the yacs config, data loaders, and DetectionCheckpointer form the surrounding plumbing.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • GeneralizedRCNN, L25 — the single nn.Module that owns the whole detection stack and branches between training forward and eval inference.
  • build_backbone, L20 — the factory that turns cfg.MODEL.BACKBONE.NAME into a concrete backbone, optionally wrapped with FPN.
  • ResNet, L362 — the classic stem-plus-four-stages backbone producing C2–C5 feature maps.
  • FPN, L17 — the Feature Pyramid Network that merges those stages into multi-scale outputs.
  • DefaultAnchorGenerator, L86 — tiles anchor boxes of configured sizes, ratios, and angles at every location of every feature level.
  • RPN, L181 — scores and regresses those anchors into a short list of object proposals.
  • StandardROIHeads, L530 — pools features on each proposal and emits classes, refined boxes, and optional masks.
  • DefaultPredictor, L284 — the one-image, one-device convenience wrapper most people meet first.

From Install to Your First Model

Installing Detectron2 means compiling a few CUDA/C++ ops against your exact PyTorch build, so the version match matters more than with a pure-Python library. The canonical path from the project’s docs is:

pip install 'git+https://github.com/facebookresearch/detectron2.git'

Assuming a matching torch and CUDA toolchain are already present, that single command builds the extensions and drops the detectron2 package into your environment. The fastest way to a first result is the DefaultPredictor, L284:

import cv2
from detectron2.config import get_cfg
from detectron2.engine import DefaultPredictor

cfg = get_cfg()
cfg.merge_from_file("COCO-InstanceSegmentation/mask_rcnn_R_50_FPN_3x.yaml")
cfg.MODEL.WEIGHTS = "detectron2://COCO-InstanceSegmentation/mask_rcnn_R_50_FPN_3x/137849600/model_final_f10217.pkl"
cfg.MODEL.DEVICE = "cpu"  # skip this line if you have a GPU

predictor = DefaultPredictor(cfg)
im = cv2.imread("input.jpg")
outputs = predictor(im)["instances"]
print(outputs.pred_boxes, outputs.pred_classes, outputs.scores)

Three lines inside DefaultPredictor.__init__ tell you the whole runtime story: build_model(self.cfg) constructs the network, DetectionCheckpointer(self.model).load(cfg.MODEL.WEIGHTS) pulls the weights (the detectron2:// scheme resolves to the model zoo CDN), and a ResizeShortestEdge transform fixes the input geometry. __call__ then converts BGR to the configured input format, resizes, and calls the model on a one-element batch. On the training side, DefaultTrainer, L355 is the opinionated counterpart: it builds the optimizer, wraps the data loaders, registers checkpoint and evaluation hooks, and inherits the hook machinery of TrainerBase, L94. For multi-GPU runs, launch, L27 either spawns one process per GPU or submits a Slurm job before invoking your main.

GeneralizedRCNN: The Meta-Architecture Glue

Everything starts at build_model, L16, which resolves cfg.MODEL.META_ARCHITECTURE against a registry and calls the class’s from_config. For GeneralizedRCNN, from_config, L72 does exactly three builds — backbone, proposal generator, and ROI heads — and returns them as constructor kwargs. There is no hidden state and no base-class magic; the model is literally the composition of those three submodules plus two registered buffers, pixel_mean and pixel_std.

The training path lives in forward, L126: normalize images via preprocess_image, L223, run self.backbone(images.tensor) to get feature maps, ask the proposal generator for proposals plus its losses, then hand features, proposals, and ground truth to the ROI heads for the detector losses. The method merges both loss dicts and returns them — no loss computation logic of its own. At eval time forward simply delegates to inference, L178, which runs the same chain without ground truth and finishes with _postprocess, L237, rescaling predicted boxes from the resized input back to the original image resolution so users never see coordinates tied to network input geometry.

Backbone and FPN: Multi-Scale Features

build_backbone, L20 reads cfg.MODEL.BACKBONE.NAME — build_resnet_backbone by default — and, when cfg.MODEL.FPN.IN_FEATURES is non-empty, wraps the result so the model consumes pyramid features instead of a single scale. The builder build_resnet_backbone, L614 maps RESNETS.DEPTH (50, 101, 152) to stem and stage specifications and assembles the ResNet, L362 object, whose make_stage, L606 helper stacks bottleneck blocks while threading input channels into output channels.

The FPN, L17 module adds 1x1 lateral convolutions over the chosen C2–C5 inputs, applies top-down upsampling, and merges the two paths with a FUSE_TYPE operation (sum or average). Its output is a dict of p2 through p6 maps, and output_shape() reports each level’s stride and channels — metadata that the anchor generator and ROI pooler later query. This division of labor is typical of the codebase: the backbone produces features, but everything downstream stays agnostic by consuming the output_shape() contract.

Proposals: Anchors, RPN Head, Top-k Selection

The proposal side is where Detectron2’s config-driven style shines. DefaultAnchorGenerator, L86 precomputes cell anchors from ANCHOR_GENERATOR.SIZES and ASPECT_RATIOS and shifts them across every position of every feature level, returning per-level anchor boxes as buffers. The RPN, L181 module then applies the shared StandardRPNHead, L67 — a 3x3 conv stack with 1x1 objectness and box-delta outputs — to each level, and passes objectness-sorted candidates through find_top_rpn_proposals, L22, which decodes deltas, clips to image bounds, drops tiny boxes, applies NMS, and keeps PRE_NMS_TOPK/POST_NMS_TOPK proposals per image (12000/2000 in training, 6000/1000 at test with defaults). Construction itself goes through build_proposal_generator, L15, so swapping RPN for a learned-proposal variant is a one-line config change.

ROI Heads and the Training Loop

Proposals become detections in the ROI stage. build_roi_heads, L38 resolves cfg.MODEL.ROI_HEADS.NAME, and StandardROIHeads, L530 implements the canonical flow: an ROIAlignV2 pooler crops each feature level at proposal coordinates, a box head classifies and refines, and optional mask and keypoint branches predict per-ROI pixel outputs. The classification edge is FastRCNNOutputLayers, L174, which owns class scores, box regression, the smooth-L1 loss, and score-threshold plus NMS inference; the mask branch is MaskRCNNConvUpsampleHead, L215, a small stack of 3x3 convs with 2x upsampling ending in a 28x28 per-class mask.

During training, StandardROIHeads samples a balanced subset of proposals against ground truth (BATCH_SIZE_PER_IMAGE, POSITIVE_FRACTION), computes box and mask losses, and returns them for forward to merge. The plumbing around this loop is equally explicit: build_detection_train_loader, L521 builds an infinite, aspect-ratio-grouped loader whose DatasetMapper applies augmentation per image, and build_detection_test_loader, L621 gives a deterministic eval loader. Persistence is centralized in DetectionCheckpointer, L16, which extends the generic Checkpointer with model-compatibility fixes and conversion shims for older Detectron and Caffe2 weights — the reason cfg.MODEL.WEIGHTS can point at files produced years ago by different frameworks.

The detail view traces the call graph: from_config builds the three children; ResNet stages feed FPN levels; anchors and the RPN head feed find_top_rpn_proposals; ROI heads pool, classify, and mask; and DefaultPredictor/DefaultTrainer wrap everything with checkpointing and data loaders.

Honest Limits

Detectron2 is explicitly research-oriented, and the repository is in maintenance mode: it is stable and widely used, but expect feature work to happen in successor projects rather than here. Treat it as a reference implementation and an experiment bench, not as a batteries-included serving framework — there is no first-class REST serving story, and production deployments typically export to TorchScript or ONNX or rebuild inference elsewhere.

The build is CUDA-centric. Custom ops compile against a specific torch/CUDA pairing, so mismatches produce long, cryptic build failures, and CPU-only or Windows setups remain awkward. Pin your torch version first, then install Detectron2 against it. None of this blocks study or experimentation — it just means you should budget setup time before the interesting part starts.

Config handling has two coexisting eras. The classic yacs yaml system — the CfgNode defaults merged with merge_from_file — powers all legacy model zoo configs, while the newer LazyConfig (plain Python objects) is the recommended path for new work. Docs and tutorials mix the two, so check which system a given config file belongs to before editing it. Finally, several model zoo and documentation links have been retired or redirected over the years; checkpoint URLs from old tutorials may need manual repair, and the detectron2:// scheme depends on CDN paths that can move. Verify weights links before wiring them into automation.

If you want the contrast, single-stage detectors tell a different story — see our yolov5 tour for a one-stage design — while the tensor-level machinery underneath Detectron2 overlaps heavily with torchvision ops, runs on the pytorch runtime, and can be exported toward onnx for deployment.
entry.summary: Walk through the Detectron2 source: the GeneralizedRCNN meta-architecture, ResNet+FPN backbones, RPN proposals, ROI heads, and the config/checkpoint plumbing.

entry.title: MediaPipe: A Source Tour of Google’s On-Device ML Framework

link.title: MediaPipe: A Source Tour of Google’s On-Device ML Framework

entry.content:
If you have ever pointed a phone camera at your own hand and watched a wireframe skeleton snap to your knuckles in real time, you have almost certainly met MediaPipe. The framework started life inside Google as a C++ engine for streaming perception and grew into the company’s default way to ship on-device ML features: face mesh, hand tracking, body pose, object detection, segmentation, and more recently on-device generative audio and text. The repository now lives under the google-ai-edge organization on GitHub, and the master branch is one of the larger codebases we have toured on this blog — thousands of build targets spanning C++, Java, Objective-C, JavaScript, and Python.

What makes MediaPipe worth reading is not any single algorithm. The landmark models are compact TFLite graphs you could also run with TensorFlow Lite or ONNX Runtime. The interesting part is everything around the model: a scheduler that moves timestamped packets between calculators, a task layer hiding it behind five friendly Python classes, and a ctypes bridge letting pure Python drive the C++ core. We read the code top-down, from the Tasks API to the framework layer, with every symbol linked to the master tree.

Two caveats up front: the PyPI package is a prebuilt wheel — building from source is a Bazel affair we treat honestly later — and you will meet two generations of Python API side by side, the classic mp.solutions modules and the newer Tasks API.

Overview of the MediaPipe source: the Tasks API classes on the left are configured by BaseOptions and running modes, talk to the native core through ctypes bindings, and all of it lands on the CalculatorGraph runtime. The legacy mp.solutions layer sits apart on the right.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • HandLandmarker, L330 — the flagship task class: 21 hand keypoints plus handedness, with a symmetric trio of entry methods we will meet below.
  • BaseOptions, L59 — the shared config every task accepts: where the model bytes come from and which delegate runs them.
  • VisionTaskRunningMode, L30 — the IMAGE / VIDEO / LIVE_STREAM enum that decides which native function signature gets called.
  • Image, L200 — the frame container handed to every task, with a zero-copy numpy_view, L376 for pixel access.
  • mediapipe_c_bindings, load_shared_library, L71 — the ctypes bridge that loads the bundled C library and wires every entry point.
  • CalculatorGraph, L109 — the C++ heart: validates a graph config, schedules nodes, and moves packets between them.
  • FlowLimiterCalculator, L72 — the unassuming calculator that keeps live streams real time by dropping stale frames.
  • SolutionBase, L186 — the legacy wrapper behind everything you reach via mp.solutions.

From Install to Your First Model

The repository README is no longer a documentation hub — it is a short stub that forwards you to the developer site at developers.google.com/edge/mediapipe. That is a small but telling change: Google treats the GitHub tree as the source of truth for code, while usage docs live elsewhere. The practical entry point remains the PyPI wheel:

pip install mediapipe

Then the canonical Tasks API incantation, assembled entirely from symbols you can verify in the tree:

import mediapipe as mp
from mediapipe.tasks import python
from mediapipe.tasks.python import vision

base_options = python.BaseOptions(model_asset_path='hand_landmarker.task')
options = vision.HandLandmarkerOptions(
    base_options=base_options,
    running_mode=vision.RunningMode.IMAGE)

with vision.HandLandmarker.create_from_options(options) as landmarker:
    mp_image = mp.Image.create_from_file('image.jpg')
    result = landmarker.detect(mp_image)

Every piece of that snippet has a home in the source. from mediapipe.tasks import python works because tasks/python/init.py, L25 re-exports BaseOptions; the vision.RunningMode alias is defined at vision/init.py, L78. The context manager is not docs sugar — enter, L593 really closes the underlying graph when the block exits. And mp.Image.create_from_file reaches a pybind factory registered in mediapipe/python/pybind/image.cc.

MediaPipe tasks consume .task bundles — TFLite model bytes plus metadata. The model_asset_path field points at a file on disk; the docstring at BaseOptions, L59 lists model_asset_buffer for raw bytes as the only other supported source. Our earlier tour of TFLite Micro covers the flatbuffer format from the microcontroller side.

The Tasks Layer: Five Classes, One Shape

The modern API’s most striking property is its uniformity. PoseLandmarker, L334, FaceLandmarker, L3083, ObjectDetector, L211 and ImageSegmenter, L232 are all built to the same template as the hand landmarker: a Result dataclass, an Options dataclass, a create_from_model_path convenience, a create_from_options factory, and three detect-style methods.

The trio of methods is the API’s real design decision. detect takes one image and blocks. detect_for_video takes an image plus a timestamp and blocks until that frame’s inference completes. detect_async takes a timestamp and a callback, returns immediately, and delivers results later — it exists only in LIVE_STREAM mode. Pass running_mode=LIVE_STREAM without a result_callback and create_from_options, L384 refuses to construct the task, validating the combination before any native call happens.

Results are plain dataclasses converted out of C structs. A HandLandmarkerResult, L246 holds lists of NormalizedLandmark, L67 — x, y, z, visibility, presence — plus world landmarks in meters and handedness categories built from Category, L24. Nothing in a result holds a reference to native memory, which is precisely the point of the conversion layer we look at next.

BaseOptions, Running Modes and the ctypes Bridge

Here is the part of the source that most MediaPipe users never see. In the current tree, the task classes do not import any pybind module. Instead, hand_landmarker.py’s import block pulls in mediapipe_c_bindings, base_options_c, and the dispatch helpers, and every native interaction goes through ctypes.

The mechanics are worth pausing on. When you construct a task, your BaseOptions dataclass is flattened into MpBaseOptionsC — a ctypes.Structure mirroring a C struct, defined in base_options_c.py — because the C ABI cannot accept a Python object. The running mode enum travels as a plain integer; the _CTYPE_VALUE_MAP at the top of the running-mode module maps IMAGE/VIDEO/LIVE_STREAM to 1/2/3. Then the C library — a single shared object shipped inside the wheel — exposes functions like hand_landmarker_detect that take those structs.

Two helpers make this safe rather than terrifying. SerialDispatcher at SerialDispatcher, L25 runs all C calls on a dedicated worker thread so that callbacks fire in order and the GIL never deadlocks against a native thread. AsyncResultDispatcher at AsyncResultDispatcher, L66 wraps live-stream callbacks so detect_async can hand you a Python-level future that resolves when the native side reports results. The Delegate enum at Delegate, L78 offers CPU and GPU, but GPU support ultimately depends on what the shipped C library was built with — one of the platform drifts we return to later.

Under the Tasks: Graphs, Calculators and Packets

Below the C ABI sits the actual MediaPipe Framework, and it is a different style of system. A CalculatorGraph, L109 consumes a CalculatorGraphConfig, L237 — a protobuf listing calculator nodes, their input and output streams, and side packets — then validates it and schedules the nodes. Data moves between calculators as Packet, L88 objects: immutable, timestamped, reference-counted payloads.

The calculator library is enormous, but one file deserves special mention for anyone doing real-time video. FlowLimiterCalculator, L72 implements back-pressure for live streams: with max_in_flight: 1, only one frame is being processed at a time, and every frame that arrives while the model is busy is dropped rather than queued. The comment block at the top of the file explains the trade-off directly — queueing video frames produces stale output and growing latency, while dropping them keeps results fresh. Every camera-facing demo graph you have seen implicitly relies on this.

The graphs behind each task are not hand-assembled at runtime. The build system composes them from .proto text graphs — the framework’s CalculatorGraphTemplate, L38 rule system expands one parametrized template into concrete configs — and ships them as binary resources inside the wheel. When a task initializes, the C library assembles the right graph and loads the model; only then does your detect call push a packet through.

The full map: task classes and their options, the container dataclasses returned as results, the serial and async dispatchers, the ctypes C-ABI layer, and the C++ framework underneath — with the legacy mp.solutions stack kept in its own group.

The Legacy solutions API Is Still There

Type mp.solutions.hands today and you get the old API — still in the tree, still shipped, but clearly from a different era. Hands, L73 subclasses SolutionBase, L186, which loads a prebuilt binary graph and feeds it numpy frames through pybind bindings. Its process(image) method at process, L300 takes a BGR numpy array and returns a named tuple, a shape that predates the dataclass discipline of the Tasks layer.

The legacy modules bundle their own conveniences — draw_landmarks, L119 draws annotated keypoints straight onto a frame — and they remain the quickest way to prototype. But they are in maintenance mode: the Tasks classes are where GPU delegates, new models, and cross-platform parity land first. If you start a new project on mp.solutions, you are building on the one generation of the API that Google has explicitly stopped evolving.

Honest Limits

Reading the source also means reading its friction, and MediaPipe has more than its share.

Building from source is a Bazel project of unusual size. The wheel you pip install is prebuilt by Google; reproducing it locally means wiring Bazel, a C++ toolchain, and platform SDKs. Contributors routinely spend more time on the build than on the code change itself.

The legacy story is genuinely confusing. mp.solutions still exists in the tree, but the model zoo for Tasks is versioned and pinned — each landmarker has a specific .task release with its own accuracy/speed variants — and Google’s docs interlink the two generations heavily. Tutorials on the internet mix APIs from both eras without saying so.

Cross-platform API drift is real. The Android Java API, the iOS Swift API, the Python Tasks API, and the web JavaScript API are separately maintained bindings over the same C++ core, and they disagree about naming, option availability, and delegate support. GPU inference, in particular, is configured differently on each platform, and a feature announced for one binding often arrives in the others late or not at all.

Finally, the Python wrapper is only as stable as its C ABI. The ctypes layer is efficient — no pybind11 shim for tasks — but it means a mismatch between the Python code and the bundled shared library fails at struct-packing time rather than import time. Pin your mediapipe version, exactly as you would pin a model.

MediaPipe remains the reference design for shipping perception ML to devices where every millisecond and megabyte counts. If you want to compare approaches, ONNX Runtime covers the general cross-platform inference story, TFLite Micro pushes the same flatbuffer ideas down to microcontrollers, and ncnn is the community-built alternative with a similar mobile focus. The graph-plus-calculators architecture, though, is the part worth stealing regardless of which runtime you end up deploying.
entry.summary: Walk through the MediaPipe source: the Tasks Python API, base options and running modes, landmarker and detector graphs, and how models ship to phones and desktops.

entry.title: Piper: A Tiny C++ Core That Speaks for Itself

link.title: Piper: A Tiny C++ Core That Speaks for Itself

entry.content:
Piper is a fast, fully local neural text-to-speech system from the Rhasspy project, the same community behind popular offline voice tooling for home automation. You hand it a sentence on standard input, it hands you a WAV file a fraction of a second later, and nothing ever leaves the machine. Voices are built on the VITS architecture, exported to ONNX, and shipped as a single .onnx file plus a small JSON sidecar. That combination is why Piper feels at home on a Raspberry Pi 4: no cloud call, no account, no GPU, and still real-time or better speech for dozens of languages.

Why read the C++ source of a TTS engine? Because Piper is one of the smallest end-to-end neural inference engines you will ever get to read in one sitting. The whole engine lives in a single piper.cpp of roughly 630 lines and a piper.hpp of about 130, plus a vendored JSON header and a 40-line WAV writer. It shows, in miniature, the same anatomy as the much larger runtimes we have toured on this blog: an ONNX Runtime session wrapped in a thin native layer, tensors assembled by hand, and fixed-point audio squeezed out at the end. If llama.cpp is the reference example of a lean native LLM runner, Piper is the equivalent for speech.

This post walks the repository through two generated architecture diagrams. Every box in the diagrams points at a real file on the master branch, and every line anchor quoted below was verified against the actual tree, so the links should survive as more than decoration.

The five neighborhoods of Piper: a CLI shell, a compact C++ core, a WAV writer, a Python runtime package, and the training side that exports voices.

Reading the overview from left to right:

The overview is best read as the life of one request, from your terminal to a speaker. Each bullet below names the exact function that carries the torch, with a verified line anchor:

  • main, L100 is the CLI shell. It reads lines from stdin forever, one utterance per line, and prints the path of every WAV it writes.
  • initialize, L216 boots espeak-ng once per process so the engine can convert raw text into IPA phonemes, and optionally loads the libtashkeel model used to diacritize Arabic.
  • loadVoice, L309 parses the JSON sidecar that ships next to every .onnx voice, filling the config structs declared in piper.hpp, L28.
  • loadModel, L262 creates the Ort::Session at L301 with deliberately austere session options tuned for fast startup rather than peak throughput.
  • synthesize, L337 packs phoneme ids, their lengths, and three scale floats into input tensors, then invokes the model once per phrase.
  • textToAudio, L446 orchestrates the speech flow: sentence splitting, phonemization via phonemize_eSpeak, L474, id mapping through phonemes_to_ids, L555, and silence insertion.
  • textToWavFile, L619 buffers the int16 samples and writes them behind a RIFF header from writeWavHeader, L27.
  • PiperVoice.load, L25 is the Python twin, a dataclass that wraps onnxruntime.InferenceSession for pip install piper-tts users.
  • export_onnx.main, L16 sits upstream of everything: it turns a PyTorch training checkpoint into the very .onnx voice the C++ side consumes.

From Install to Your First Model

The fastest route is a release tarball. Piper ships prebuilt binaries for Windows, macOS, Linux on x86_64 and armhf, and each archive carries an espeak-ng-data directory next to the executable, which is exactly where main.cpp looks for it, L156. Download a voice pair from the HuggingFace model hub, for example en_US-amy-medium.onnx and its .onnx.json sidecar, then:

echo 'Welcome to local text to speech.' | piper -m en_US-amy-medium.onnx -f welcome.wav

Behind that one-liner, three things happen in order. First, parseArgs in main.cpp, L457 validates that both the model and its sidecar exist, defaulting the config path to the model path plus .json. Second, loadVoice reads the sidecar with the vendored json.hpp parser and extracts the phoneme_id_map, the speaker count, the sample rate, and three synthesis knobs. Third, espeak-ng is initialized and the ONNX model is memory-mapped into a session. The stdin loop then synthesizes your line and reports a real-time factor, the ratio of inference seconds to audio seconds, at main.cpp, L355. On a Raspberry Pi 4 that factor hovers around 1 to 2 for medium voices, which is why the project markets itself as real-time on the Pi.

The defaults are worth a glance because they are the knobs you will tweak first. SynthesisConfig, L52 fixes noiseScale at 0.667, lengthScale at 1.0, and noiseW at 0.8, with a 22050 Hz mono 16-bit output shape. lengthScale above 1.0 slows the delivery down, and --sentence_silence pads pauses between sentences. Multi-speaker voices resolve --speaker names through a speaker_id_map, and the --json-input mode lets a caller pass text, speaker, and output path as one JSON object per line, which is how Home Assistant and similar integrations drive the binary.

Python developers get the same engine through the wheel. The src/python_run package exposes exactly one symbol, PiperVoice, re-exported from __init__.py. PiperVoice.load builds an onnxruntime.InferenceSession with the CPU provider by default and a CUDA provider when asked, and synthesize_stream_raw yields raw PCM bytes sentence by sentence, so you can wrap it in wave or push it straight to an audio device. A companion downloader in download.py fetches voices and verifies their hashes, and an optional HTTP server wraps the whole thing for networked setups.

Before committing to a voice, you can measure rather than guess. The src/benchmark folder contains small scripts, including benchmark_onnx.py and benchmark_torchscript.py, that replay the same test sentences against an exported model and report inference timing per utterance. They use the identical four-name tensor contract as the shipped runtimes, so their numbers translate directly to what the C++ binary will experience on your hardware. For a median voice and a mid-range laptop CPU, expect a real-time factor comfortably above 1, and on the Pi treat medium-quality voices as the sweet spot between size and clarity.

Inside the Detail Diagram

The detail diagram zooms into the two bodies of code that matter: the C++ engine on one side, and the Python package pair on the other.

The synthesis chain in close-up: config structs feed a session-bearing ModelSession, synthesize builds tensors for one Run call, and the Python runtime mirrors the same tensor contract.

Follow the C++ column downward. initialize calls espeak_Initialize, L221 in synchronous mode, meaning espeak never writes audio, it only answers phoneme queries. loadVoice splits the sidecar parse across three functions, parsePhonemizeConfig, L47, parseSynthesisConfig, L135, and parseModelConfig, L197, each tolerant of missing keys. loadModel then disables graph optimizations, the CPU memory arena, memory patterns, and profiling, a tradeoff documented in comments at L275 as roughly halving model load time with no visible inference benefit. That choice is very Piper: optimize for the second a user waits, not the millisecond a server saves.

synthesize is the heart. It allocates three or four tensors matching the interface fixed by the exporter, names hard-coded at L380 as input, input_lengths, scales, and the optional sid, then fires one session.onnx.Run, L386 call. The output float tensor is peak-normalized and clamped into int16 samples at L411, which keeps the audio path allocation-light and the WAV format trivial. textToWavFile, L619 then writes the header through wavfile.hpp, L6 and streams the buffer to any std::ostream, which is how --output_file - can dump sound straight to stdout.

The Python column is a faithful mirror, not a wrapper. PiperVoice.phonemize, L57 calls the same piper-phonemize routines the C++ build links against, phonemes_to_ids, L72 frames each sentence with the BOS, EOS, and PAD sentinels defined in const.py, L3, and synthesize_ids_to_raw, L140 feeds the identical four-name tensor contract, culminating in the run call at L183. If you have read our ONNX primer, the input names will look familiar, because exported VITS graphs pin their interface at export time.

Why the Two Implementations Stay in Sync

The trick that keeps C++ and Python agreeing is that neither owns the speech flow’s contract. The exporter owns it. During training, the VITS model in vits/models.py, L522 exposes an infer entry point at L681, and the exporter traces through it so the ONNX graph expects exactly the tensors the C++ side later builds. The PyTorch Lightning shell in vits/lightning.py, L20 handles optimization and epochs, then hands the weights over. A reference consumer in infer_onnx.py, L19 exercises the exported graph with the same input names, closing the loop before any release. This division, one exporter defining the interface and many thin runtimes consuming it, is a pattern you can lift into your own projects, and it is the same idea that lets projects like Ollama and MediaPipe serve one model format from many bindings.

The voice ecosystem completes the picture. Training itself is driven through the notebooks at the repo root, where a multilingual training notebook and an ONNX inference notebook walk from raw audio clips to a finished .onnx voice, and the preprocessing step in preprocess.py, L43 turns transcripts into the phoneme-id datasets the trainer consumes. Everything downstream of that point is deliberately frozen: once export_onnx.py writes the graph, the C++ core, the Python wheel, and the benchmark scripts all treat it as an immutable artifact with a published interface. That freeze is what allows a voice trained on a GPU workstation in PyTorch to speak on a Pi through six hundred lines of C++ it has never seen.

Honest Limits

No source tour is complete without the caveats, and Piper wears its constraints openly in the code.

  • The audio format is hard-wired. The WAV writer assumes 16-bit samples, with blockAlign and bitsPerSample fixed at wavfile.hpp, L18, and the C++ path rescales every output to int16. If your voice exports a different sample width, the C++ runner will not follow you.
  • There is no token streaming in the C++ binary. --output-raw streams finished phrase buffers through a background thread at rawOutputProc, L371, but latency is per phrase, not per sample. True incremental synthesis would require the streaming export variants that live, experimentally, in the training tree.
  • Compute defaults to CPU. A --use-cuda flag appends the CUDA execution provider at L268, but there is no DirectML, Core ML, or Vulkan path in the C++ core, so exotic accelerators are out of scope by design.
  • Phoneme coverage is only as good as espeak-ng. Unknown phonemes are counted and warned about at L600, not invented, which is honest but means unusual scripts can degrade to silences or approximations.
  • It is not a training framework. src/python/piper_train is a separate heavyweight dependency tree for making voices; the C++ and python_run packages are consumers only.
  • The repo ships a voice config and a test model under etc/, but all real voices live on HuggingFace, so first use requires a download, and the --espeak_data path matters when you relocate the binary.

None of these limits are hidden, and most are direct consequences of the design goal: a TTS engine small enough to start instantly on a $50 computer, with the entire speech flow legible in under a thousand lines. That legibility is the real gift of the codebase. Between the overview and the detail diagram you have now seen where text becomes phonemes, where phonemes become ids, where ids become floats, and where floats become the bytes your speaker plays, all anchored to lines you can open in one click.
entry.summary: A source tour of rhasspy/piper: how its compact C++ engine turns text into phonemes, runs a VITS voice in ONNX Runtime, and streams 16-bit PCM audio, with two architecture diagrams.

entry.title: Swin Transformer: A Source Tour of Microsoft’s Hierarchical Vision Backbone

link.title: Swin Transformer: A Source Tour of Microsoft’s Hierarchical Vision Backbone

entry.content:
When the Swin Transformer landed in 2021, most vision transformers were still computing attention over every pair of tokens in the image — quadratic cost, single-scale feature maps, and an awkward fit for dense prediction tasks that expect pyramid-shaped backbones. Microsoft’s answer, written by Ze Liu and collaborators, was to restrict self-attention to small local windows and then shift those windows by half their size every other block, so information still flows across the whole image. The result became the default backbone for a generation of detection and segmentation systems, including the Detectron2 ecosystem, and its hierarchical four-stage design still shows up in modern architectures.

What makes this repository especially worth reading is that the ideas map onto the code with almost no abstraction layer. There is one file, models/swin_transformer.py, that contains the entire model: patch embedding, windowed attention, shifted-window masking, patch merging, and the classification head. Around it sit a thin yacs-based config system, a data loading module built on PyTorch and timm primitives, and a distributed training entry that was clearly written to run on 8-GPU ImageNet boxes. Reading it top to bottom teaches you not just Swin, but how production vision training repos were structured in that era.

In this tour we walk the source the way a maintainer would: the model file first, then the shifted-window mechanics, the downsampling stage, the checkpoint loading quirks, and finally the training entry. Two diagrams generated from the actual repository tree anchor the discussion.

Overview of the repo: main.py orchestrates config, data, optimizer, and scheduler, while models/build.py instantiates the SwinTransformer backbone from models/swin_transformer.py.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • SwinTransformer, L485 — the top-level nn.Module that assembles patch embedding, four stages, final norm, and the linear head.
  • PatchEmbed, L437 — a strided 4×4 Conv2d that chops the image into non-overlapping patches and flattens them into tokens.
  • BasicLayer, L364 — one stage of the hierarchy: a stack of blocks followed by optional downsampling.
  • SwinTransformerBlock, L175 — the workhorse block that alternates regular and shifted window attention around an MLP.
  • WindowAttention, L77 — multi-head self-attention confined to an M×M window, with a learned relative position bias table.
  • PatchMerging, L315 — the resolution-halving layer that gives Swin its pyramid shape.
  • build_model, L15 — a config-driven dispatcher that also knows about Swin-V2, Swin-MoE, and Swin-MLP variants.
  • main, L90 — the distributed training and evaluation entry that wires everything together.
  • load_pretrained, L45 — the fine-tuning loader that repairs mismatched weights, including bicubic resizing of the bias tables.

Why Windows Instead of Global Attention

The motivating trade-off is cost. Global self-attention over H×W/16 tokens scales quadratically with image size, which is brutal for detection backbones that must process 800×1333 feature maps. Swin instead partitions the feature map into non-overlapping windows of default size M=7 and attends only within each window, making the cost linear in the number of tokens. The helper functions window_partition, L45 and window_reverse, L60 are just view/permute reshapes that move between (B, H, W, C) and a batch of (num_windows*B, M, M, C) tensors — no fancy kernels required for the baseline path.

The catch is that attention confined to fixed windows has no communication across window borders. Swin’s fix is the shifted window scheme: even-numbered blocks use regular windows (W-MSA), odd-numbered blocks shift the feature map by ⌊M/2⌋ pixels along both axes first. After the shift, windows straddle the boundaries of the previous layer’s windows, so tokens from different regions end up in the same attention group. You can see this in SwinTransformerBlock.forward at the cyclic shift, L260, where torch.roll moves the feature map, and in BasicLayer’s construction at L397, which alternates shift_size=0 with shift_size=window_size//2 across blocks.

Rolling creates one artifact: a window that wraps around the image edge contains tokens that are not actually spatial neighbors. Rather than wasting compute on those connections, the block precomputes an attention mask in its constructor (register_buffer("attn_mask", ...), L245) that adds −100 to cross-region attention logits, effectively zeroing them after softmax. The mask is a buffer, not a parameter, so it is recomputed per resolution and — importantly — deleted by the checkpoint loader rather than restored from disk.

The Anatomy of a Shifted Window Block

Each SwinTransformerBlock follows the classic pre-norm transformer recipe with two sublayers. The first applies LayerNorm, optionally rolls the feature map, partitions windows, and calls WindowAttention, L77. The second is a GELU MLP with a 4× expansion, implemented in the modest Mlp, L26 class. Both sublayers are wrapped in residual connections with stochastic-depth (DropPath) regularization.

Inside WindowAttention, three details deserve attention. First, the QKV projection is a single nn.Linear(dim, dim*3) followed by a reshape into heads — standard, but note the explicit q * self.scale before the matmul, since this code predates PyTorch’s fused scaled_dot_product_attention. Second, the attention logits get a learned bias added: the relative_position_bias_table, L101 is a (2M−1)² × num_heads parameter table, and a precomputed relative_position_index buffer maps each of the M²×M² token pairs inside a window to one row of that table. This relative bias is what lets the model know where tokens sit within their window without any absolute positional embedding. Third, the block exposes no_weight_decay_keywords at L585 so the optimizer excludes this table from weight decay — a small but consequential training detail handled in build_optimizer, L19.

The optimizer code itself is worth a skim. set_weight_decay, L59 splits parameters into decay/no-decay groups based on parameter shape (1-D tensors like norms get zero decay) and the skip lists above. On the schedule side, build_scheduler, L16 wraps timm’s cosine scheduler with a linear warmup, and the repo also ships a homegrown LinearLRScheduler, L66 for recipes that prefer linear decay. The entry point then linearly scales the learning rate with total batch size at main.py L327, a convention from the large-batch ImageNet training era.

PatchMerging and the Four-Stage Hierarchy

Where ViT keeps one resolution throughout, Swin builds a pyramid that CNN-based detectors expect: resolutions H/4, H/8, H/16, H/32 with channel widths doubling at each stage. The glue between stages is PatchMerging. Its forward pass at PatchMerging.forward, L331 slices the feature map into even/odd rows and columns, concatenates the four neighbors along the channel dimension (2C becomes 4C), applies LayerNorm, and then a linear layer without bias that projects 4C back down to 2C. Resolution halves, width doubles — exactly the role a strided convolution plays in ResNet.

The SwinTransformer constructor at L529 wires this up by instantiating one BasicLayer per stage, passing downsample=PatchMerging for every stage except the last. Each BasicLayer builds depths[i] blocks with alternating shift sizes, and optionally wraps each block in gradient checkpointing when use_checkpoint is set — a memory saver that matters for the 384-resolution and Swin-L configurations. After the final stage, forward_features, L588 applies a final LayerNorm, average-pools over tokens, and hands the feature vector to the classification head. Because every piece is a plain module with a flops() method, the repo reports GFLOPs for any configuration at startup.

Checkpoint Loading and Relative Position Remapping

The subtlety in this repo is that several “parameters” of a Swin model are actually resolution-dependent buffers: relative_position_index, attn_mask, and the size of relative_position_bias_table itself. That means a checkpoint trained at 224×224 cannot be loaded verbatim into a 384×384 model. The fine-tuning loader load_pretrained, L45 handles this with surgical string matching over state-dict keys.

First it deletes all relative_position_index and attn_mask entries, since those are always re-initialized from the new model’s geometry (L51 onward). Then, for each relative_position_bias_table whose row count changed, it bicubically interpolates the pretrained table to the new (2M−1)² size — the remap logic lives at L66. Finally, if the classifier head mismatches, it does something clever for the ImageNet-22K → 1K transfer: rather than re-initializing, it reads data/map22kto1k.txt, a fixed 21841→1000 index map, and slices the pretrained head rows accordingly (L111). That one file explains how the 22K-pretrained checkpoints reach their published 1K accuracies out of the box. The resume path, load_checkpoint, L18, is the ordinary strict-shape restore of model, optimizer, scheduler, and AMP scaler for interrupted runs.

From Install to Your First Model

The get_started guide targets CUDA 10.2-era environments and pins old versions deliberately — the code relies on timm internals that changed after 0.4.12. The setup sequence is:

conda create -n swin python=3.7 -y
conda activate swin
conda install pytorch==1.8.0 torchvision==0.9.0 cudatoolkit=10.2 -c pytorch
pip install timm==0.4.12
pip install opencv-python==4.4.0.46 termcolor==1.1.0 yacs==0.1.8 pyyaml scipy

The repo never grew a requirements.txt on its main branch; the guide pins each dependency explicitly instead, so treat those five lines as the source of truth. With a torch build of your choosing, the fastest way to touch the model is a single-GPU evaluation of the Swin-B checkpoint:

python -m torch.distributed.launch --nproc_per_node 1 --master_port 12345 main.py --eval \
  --cfg configs/swin/swin_base_patch4_window7_224.yaml \
  --resume swin_base_patch4_window7_224.pth --data-path <imagenet-path>

Training uses the same entry with --cfg configs/swin/swin_tiny_patch4_window7_224.yaml and --nproc_per_node 8, as documented in the guide’s ImageNet-1K section. Under the hood, parse_option, L36 merges CLI flags into the yacs defaults via get_config, L352, which in turn loads the chosen YAML through _update_config_from_file, L268. Data flows through build_loader, L44, which selects between torchvision-style folders, a cached in-memory variant, and the ImageNet-22K archive reader in data/, then attaches mixup/CutMix from the timm data module. One epoch of the training loop, train_one_epoch, L174, uses AMP mixed precision through a wrapped grad scaler and logs lr, loss, grad norm, and memory each step; validate, L235 reports top-1/top-5 on the val split. Note that torch.distributed.launch is deprecated in modern PyTorch — with torch 2.x the code switches to reading LOCAL_RANK from the environment, per the comment at main.py L70.

The detailed view adds the attention internals, data loading, optimizer/scheduler construction, and the checkpoint utilities in utils.py.

Honest Limits

Treat this repository as a paper-replica research artifact from 2021–2022, not a maintained library. It is effectively archived: the last significant updates landed in mid-2022. The training recipes assume serious hardware — the published ImageNet numbers come from 8× V100-class GPUs, and the ImageNet-22K pre-training runs are well beyond a single workstation, even with gradient checkpointing and --accumulation-steps. The dependency pins are the other friction point: timm==0.4.12 is ancient, and importing the model with current timm versions breaks on the timm.models.layers import path (modern timm moved it to timm.layers). If you want Swin weights in a maintained stack, timm re-implements every Swin variant with its own builder and pretrain tags, and the Hugging Face torchvision releases include shifted-window backbones for detection work.

Architecturally, Swin has been superseded twice over: the same group’s Swin-V2 (also in this repo, under models/swin_transformer_v2.py) replaced the bias table with a log-spaced coordinate function to handle larger windows, and the field has since moved to hybrid and plain ViT designs. None of this changes the historical verdict: Swin’s windowed hierarchical design made transformers practical as drop-in CNN replacements, and this codebase remains the clearest executable specification of that idea.
entry.summary: Walk through the Swin source: shifted-window self-attention with relative position bias, patch merging downsampling, checkpoint weight remapping, and the training entry.

entry.title: TensorFlow Serving: A Source Tour of Google’s Model Server

link.title: TensorFlow Serving: A Source Tour of Google’s Model Server

entry.content:
TensorFlow Serving is Google’s open-source model server: the piece of infrastructure that takes a trained TensorFlow model off a researcher’s laptop and makes it answer real network traffic, reliably, at low latency. You export a SavedModel into a versioned directory, point the server at the parent folder, and it discovers every numbered version, loads the newest one, swaps versions atomically while old requests drain, and answers Predict, Classify, Regress, and GetModelMetadata calls over both gRPC and an HTTP/REST endpoint. It ships as a single prebuilt binary, tensorflow_model_server, published through apt packages and Docker images, and it has quietly run a large share of Google’s internal inference traffic for years.

Why bother reading its source at all? Because this is one of the few production-grade serving systems written almost entirely in C++, and the code is organized around a small set of interfaces — Source, SourceAdapter, Loader, Manager — that compose into a genuinely elegant component model. Once you see how those pieces snap together, you understand not just this server but the general anatomy of every model server you will ever touch. It also makes a sharp contrast with the Python-centric stacks we have covered before, like TorchServe, and with the multi-framework Triton Server, both of which lean on Python or backend-specific runtimes where TensorFlow Serving compiles everything down to one C++ process.

This post is a source tour, not a tutorial. Every symbol below links to a real file and line on the master branch, and the two architecture diagrams were generated directly from the actual repository tree. We will follow the server from main() all the way to a batched session execution, then close with the practical bits — installation, first model, and the limits you will hit in production.

What the Server Must Solve

Before diving into files, it helps to enumerate the problems a model server has to solve, because every directory in the repository maps to one of them. First, discovery: new model versions appear on disk (or on GCS or S3) while the server is running, and something must notice. Second, versioning policy: when version 7 shows up while version 6 still serves traffic, the server needs rules for when to load 7, when to unload 6, and what to do if loading 7 fails. Third, loading itself: a SavedModel must be deserialized into a session with its graph, signature definitions, and variables, and that load can take minutes for large models. Fourth, efficiency: single requests are wasteful for GPUs, so the server can coalesce concurrent requests into batches. Fifth, presentation: gRPC, REST, health checks, and monitoring endpoints all need to expose the same underlying manager state.

The repository layout mirrors this list almost exactly. tensorflow_serving/sources/ contains things that watch the outside world, tensorflow_serving/core/ contains the version-management machinery, tensorflow_serving/servables/tensorflow/ knows how to turn a SavedModel into something callable, tensorflow_serving/batching/ implements request coalescing, and tensorflow_serving/model_servers/ glues everything into the binary you actually run. That symmetry between problem and directory is the first sign of a well-factored codebase, and it is what makes the diagrams below readable.

The TensorFlow Serving stack, from the command-line entry point through model discovery, version management, and the batched request path.

Reading the overview from left to right:

  • main, L82 is where the binary starts. It declares roughly forty command-line flags — port, model_base_path, batching parameters, session parallelism — into an Options struct and hands it to the server builder at main, L342.
  • Server::BuildAndStart, L182 creates the ServerCore, registers the gRPC services, optionally starts the REST frontend, and then blocks in WaitForTermination, L464 until shutdown.
  • ServerCore::Create, L260 is the true orchestrator. Its Initialize, L306 method builds the three moving parts — source, adapters, manager — and WaitUntilModelsAvailable, L328 keeps startup blocked until every configured model is actually servable.
  • On the discovery side, FileSystemStoragePathSource::Create, L373 starts a polling thread; PollFileSystemForConfig, L329 scans each base path for numerically named subdirectories, and PollFileSystemAndInvokeCallback, L444 pushes the result as aspired versions.
  • SavedModelBundleSourceAdapter::Create, L36 builds the adapter that converts each aspired storage path into a loadable servable, wiring the adapter chain the core requested in CreateAdapters, L728.
  • SavedModelBundleFactory::CreateSavedModelBundle, L116 does the heavy lifting: it loads the meta-graph, session, and signature map, then optionally replays recorded traffic via RunSavedModelWarmup, L82 so the first real request is not slow.
  • On the management side, ServerCore::CreateAspiredVersionsManager, L785 builds the AspiredVersionsManager, L85, the state machine that owns every loaded and loading servable in the process.
  • That manager orders candidates with a pluggable policy — the model server default is AvailabilityPreservingPolicy, L39, which never unloads the currently serving version until its successor is fully ready.
  • Finally, the request path: PredictionServiceImpl::Predict, L38 receives the gRPC call, acquires a scoped ServableHandle, L75 through Manager::GetUntypedServableHandle, L109, and executes the signature via the predictor in TensorflowPredictor::Predict, L33.

Inside the Loading Flow

The overview deliberately hides the most interesting machinery: what exactly happens between “a new version directory appeared” and “requests now flow to it”. The detail diagram expands that seam, and it is where the design earns its reputation.

The detailed view: adapter wiring, the manager and its policies, per-servable harnesses, state monitoring, and the batching layer wrapped around the session.

Start with the adapter contract. Everything that feeds models into the manager is a Source, L65 — a thing that pushes aspired versions to a callback. A SourceAdapter, L60 is a source that transforms another source’s output, and the storage-path-to-SavedModel chain is exactly two such hops: the file system source emits StoragePath items, an adapter turns them into loadable servables. ServerCore::CreateRouter, L696 inserts a dynamic router between them so each model name reaches only its own adapter.

Inside the manager, every candidate version is wrapped in a LoaderHarness, L52, a tiny state machine that moves each servable through new, loading, ready, and unloading states while guarding transitions against races. The harness drives a Loader, L57, whose Load() at Load, L90 materializes the model. Crucially, Loader::EstimateResources() lets the manager decide whether the new version even fits before starting the load; the estimate comes from EstimateResourceFromPath, L92 in the SavedModel case.
